question: The total momentum of electrons in a straight wire of length 1000 m carrying a current of 70 A is closest to.
solution:
Let $A$ be the uniform cross-sectional area of the wire,

$n$ be the number density of conduction electrons (electrons per unit volume)

$e$ be the elementary charge ($e \approx 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$)

$m$ be the mass of an electron ($m \approx 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$)

$v_d$ be the drift velocity of the electrons

The total volume of the wire is $V = A \cdot L$

Then total number of conduction electrons $N$ present in the wire is, $N = n \cdot V = n \cdot A \cdot L$

Each electron drifts with velocity $v_d$, so its individual momentum due to drift is $p_e = m v_d$

Assuming the random thermal velocities sum to zero on average, the total momentum $P$ of all free electrons in the wire is

P = N \cdot m v_d = (n A L) \cdot m v_d

P = \frac{m}{e} \times (n e A v_d) \times L

The electric current $I$ passing through the cross-section is $I = n e A v_d$

P = \frac{m}{e} \cdot I \cdot L

The length of the wire is $L = 1000\ \mathrm{m}$

The current in the wire is $I = 70\ \mathrm{A}$

Substituting the values,

P = \frac{9.1 \times 10^{-31}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \times 70 \times 1000 = 5.6875 \times 10^{-12} \times 7 \times 10^{4}

P = 5.6875 \times 10^{-12} \times 7 \times 10^{4} = 39.8125 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{N\cdot s}

P \approx 40 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{N - sec}

Thus, the correct option is (A).

question: Length of a rod is d and cross-section area A as shown in the figure. A steady current i flows through the rod. Number of free electrons (carrying current) per unit volume changes linearly from $n_0$ to $2n_0$ with distance x from left end to right end. Then average drift velocity of electrons (averaged over the distance travelled in the rod) will be :
solution:
The left end of the rod is at $\mathrm{x}=0$ and the right end is at $\mathrm{x}=1$.

The number density of free electrons changes linearly with x from $\mathrm{n}_0$ at $\mathrm{x}=0$ to $2 \mathrm{n}_0$ at $\mathrm{x}=1$.

A linear function has the general form $\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{x})=\mathrm{mx}+\mathrm{c}$

At $\mathrm{x}=0: \mathrm{n}(0)=\mathrm{c}=\mathrm{n}_0$

At $\mathrm{x}=1: \mathrm{n}(\mathrm{l})=\mathrm{m} \cdot \mathrm{d}+\mathrm{n}_0=2 \mathrm{n}_0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~m}=\mathrm{n}_0 \mathrm{l}$

So, the function of free electrons $\mathrm{n}=\mathrm{n}_0+\frac{\mathrm{n}_0}{\mathrm{~d}} \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{n}_0\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{x}}{1}\right)$

For a cross-section of area A at position x. In a steady state, the current i is constant across every section of the rod.

In a time interval $\Delta \mathrm{t}$, conduction electrons moving at drift speed $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}}$ travels a distance $\Delta \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}} \Delta \mathrm{t}$.

So, the volume swept by these electrons is \Delta V = A \cdot \Delta x = A \cdot v_d \, \Delta t

The total charge passing through this cross-section in time $\Delta t$ is

\Delta q = [n(x) \cdot \Delta V] \, e = n(x) \, e \, A \, v_d \, \Delta t

As current $i$ is the charge flowing per unit time,

i = \frac{\Delta q}{\Delta t} = n(x) \, e \, A \, v_d

v_d = \frac{i}{neA}

Substitute $n=n_0\left(1+\frac{x}{1}\right)$, the expression for drift velocity of electron at $x$ is $v_d=\frac{i}{n_0 e A\left(1+\frac{x}{1}\right)}$

The average of a function $f(x)$ over an interval from $0$ to $l$ is

\langle v_d \rangle = \frac{1}{l} \int\limits_{0}^{l} v_d\, dx

$\left\langle\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{\mathrm{l}} \int_0^{\mathrm{l}} \frac{\mathrm{i}}{\mathrm{n}_0 \mathrm{eA}\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{l}}\right)} \mathrm{dx}$

Let $u = 1 + \frac{x}{l}$, so $du = \frac{1}{l}\,dx \rightarrow dx = l\,du$.

When $x = 0$, $u = 1$.

When $x = l$, $u = 1 + 1 = 2$.

\langle v_d \rangle = \frac{i}{n_0 e A l} \int\limits_{1}^{2} l \times \frac{1}{u}\, du = \frac{i}{n_0 e A} \int\limits_{1}^{2} \frac{1}{u}\, du

\langle v_d \rangle = \frac{i}{n_0 e A} [\ln u]_{1}^{2} = \frac{i}{n_0 e A} [\ln 2 - \ln 1] = \frac{i}{n_0 e A} \ln 2

Thus, the correct option is (C).

question: The drift velocity of electrons in a conducting wire is of the order of 1 mm/s yet the bulb glows very quickly after the switch is put on because
options: the random speed of electrons is very high of the order of $10^6$ m/s
the electrons transfer their energy very quickly through collisions
electric field is set up in the wire very quickly, producing a current through each cross-section, almost instantaneously
solution:
When an electrical circuit switch is closed, a potential difference is established between the terminals. This does not mean an electron from the switch has to physically travel through the wire all the way to the bulb for the filament to start glowing.

The disturbance in the electrostatic field (due to electrons) is propagated along the conducting wire in the form of an electromagnetic wave at a speed comparable to the speed of light in that medium.

\mathbf{v}_{\text {signal }} \approx \mathbf{c} \sim \mathbf{1 0}^{\mathbf{8}} \mathbf{m} / \mathbf{s}

Because this electric field $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{E}}$ is along the entire length of the wire instantaneously, an electrostatic force $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{F}}=-\mathbf{e} \overrightarrow{\mathbf{E}}$ acts simultaneously on every free conduction electron present throughout the whole circuit, including the electrons inside the filament of the bulb.

Consequently, electrons everywhere begin drifting almost at the same instant, establishing a current across every cross-section of the wire without waiting for electrons to physically travel from the power source to the load.

Hence, option (c) is correct.

Random thermal motion of electrons is around $\mathbf{1 0}^{\mathbf{5}}-\mathbf{1 0}^{\mathbf{6}} \mathbf{~ m} / \mathbf{s}$, but it has zero net vector displacement and cannot account for directional energy delivery to the bulb. Hence, option (a) is not correct.

Mechanical collision transfer is not what propagates the signal; it is the electromagnetic field propagation. Hence, option (b) is not correct.

Thus, the correct option is (C).

question: Find the average drift speed of conduction electrons in a copper wire of cross-sectional area $1.0 \times 10^{-7} \; \mathrm{m}^2$ carrying a current of $1.5 \; \mathrm{A}$. Assume that each copper atom contributes roughly one conduction electron. The density of copper is $9.0 \times 10^{3} \; \mathrm{kg}\; \mathrmm^{-3}$ and its atomic mass is $63.5 \; \mathrm{u}$.
solution:
For a cylindrical segment of a conductor with cross-sectional area A .

Let n be the number of conduction electrons per unit volume, e be the magnitude of charge on an electron ( $\mathrm{e} \approx\left.1.6 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{C}\right)$ and $v_d$ be the average drift speed of the electrons.

In a small time interval $\Delta t$, each electron drifts along the wire by a distance.

\Delta x = v_d\,\Delta t

The volume containing the conduction electrons that pass across a given cross-section in this interval is

\Delta V = A \cdot \Delta x = A\,v_d\,\Delta t

The total number of electrons in this volume is

N = n\,\Delta V = nA\,v_d\,\Delta t

The net charge transferred across the cross-section is

\Delta q = Ne = neA\,v_d\,\Delta t

The electric current $I$ is the rate of charge flow.

I = \frac{\Delta q}{\Delta t} = \frac{neA\,v_d\,\Delta t}{\Delta t} = neA\,v_d

v_d = \frac{I}{neA}

The mass density of copper is

d = 9.0 \times 10^3\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}

The molar mass of copper is given as

M = 63.5\ \mathrm{g/mol} = 63.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg/mol}

The Avogadro's constant is

N_A \approx 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \mathrm{atoms/mol}

For a unit volume ($V = 1\ \mathrm{m^3}$) of copper, the mass of this unit volume is;

m=d\times 1=9.0\times 10^3\ \mathrm{kg}

The number of moles of copper in this mass is

\text{moles}=\frac{m}{M}=\frac{d}{M}

The total number of copper atoms per unit volume is $n_{\text{atom}}=\frac{d}{M}\times N_A$

Since each copper atom contributes roughly one conduction electron

n=n_{\text{atom}}=\frac{d\cdot N_A}{M}

Substituting the numerical values,

n=\frac{(9.0\times 10^3)(6.022\times 10^{23})}{63.5\times 10^{-3}}

n=\frac{54.198\times 10^{26}}{63.5\times 10^{-3}}\approx 8.535\times 10^{28}\ \text{electrons/m}^3

The amount of current is $I=1.5\ \mathrm{A}$

Cross-sectional area, $A=1.0\times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}^2$

Substituting $n$, $I$, $A$, and $e$ into the drift speed formula,

v_d=\frac{1.5}{(8.535\times 10^{28})(1.6\times 10^{-19})(1.0\times 10^{-7})}

13.656\times 10^2=1365.6\ \mathrm{C/m}

v_d=\frac{1.5}{1365.6}\approx 1.098\times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m/s}

v_d\approx 1.1\ \mathrm{mm/s}

Thus, the correct option is (A)

question: In a straight conductor of uniform cross-section charge $q$ is flowing for time $t$. Let $s$ be the specific charge of an electron. The momentum of all the free electrons per unit length of the conductor, due to their drift velocity only, is
solution:
Specific charge (s) of a particle is the ratio of its charge magnitude to its mass $s=\frac{e}{m}$

Where e is the charge of an electron and m is the mass of an electron.

\Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{~s}}

The steady electric current I flowing through the conductor when a charge q passes in time t is $\mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{t}}$

Let A be the uniform cross-sectional area of the conductor, L be the length of the conductor, n be the number density of conduction electrons (electrons per unit volume) and $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}}$ be the drift velocity of the electrons.

In a time interval $\Delta \mathrm{t}$, the electrons drift a distance $\Delta \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}} \Delta \mathrm{t}$.

The volume swept by these charges across a section is $\Delta \mathrm{V}=\mathrm{A} \cdot \Delta \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{A} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}} \Delta \mathrm{t}$

The charge passing through the section in time $\Delta \mathrm{t}$ is $\Delta \mathrm{q}=(\mathrm{n} \Delta \mathrm{V}) \mathrm{e}=\mathrm{n} \mathrm{eAv}_{\mathrm{d}} \Delta \mathrm{t}$

Hence, the current I is $\mathrm{I}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{q}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\mathrm{neAv}_{\mathrm{d}}$

For the entire length L of the conductor, the total volume of this segment is $\mathrm{V}_{\text {total }}=\mathrm{A} \cdot \mathrm{L}$.

The total number of free conduction electrons in this length is $\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{n} \cdot \mathrm{V}_{\text {total }}=\mathrm{nAL}$

Each electron has a drift momentum $\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{e}}=\mathrm{m} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}}$

Therefore, the total momentum P of all free conduction electrons in length L due to drift is:

\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{e}}=(\mathrm{nAL})\left(\mathrm{m} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{e}}\left(\mathrm{n} \text { e } \mathrm{A} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}}\right) \mathrm{L}

Substituting $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{n}$ e $\mathrm{A} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}}$ into the equation $\mathrm{P}=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{e}} \cdot \mathrm{I} \cdot \mathrm{L}$

So, the momentum per unit length, $\left(\mathrmp^{\prime}\right)$ is $\mathrmp^{\prime}=\frac{\mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{L}}=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{e}} \cdot \mathrm{I}$

Substituting $\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{e}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{~s}}$ and $\mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{t}} \Rightarrow \mathrmp^{\prime}=\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{~s}}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{t}}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{ts}}$

Thus, the correct option is (A).

question: Two cylindrical rods of uniform cross-section radii $r$ and $2r$, having free electrons per unit volume $2n$ and $n$ respectively are joined in series. A current $I$ flows through them in steady state. Then, the ratio of drift velocity of free electron in left rod to drift velocity of electron in the right rod is $\left(\frac{v_L}{v_R}\right)$ is
solution:
Let a cylindrical conductor of cross-sectional area A, carrying a steady current I.

Let $\mathrm{n}=$ number of free electrons per unit volume (electron density)

e = magnitude of electron charge

If $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}}=$ drift velocity of the electrons, then in a time interval $\Delta \mathrm{t}$, the distance moved by drifting electrons along the conductor is $\Delta \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}} \Delta \mathrm{t}$

The volume occupied by these moving charges is $\Delta \mathrm{V}=\mathrm{A} \cdot \Delta \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{A} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}} \Delta \mathrm{t}$

The total charge $\Delta \mathrm{Q}$ passing through the cross-section in time $\Delta \mathrm{t}$ is

\Delta \mathrm{Q}=(\mathrm{n} \Delta \mathrm{~V}) \mathrm{e}=\mathrm{neA} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}} \Delta \mathrm{t}

Electric current I is the rate of charge flow $\mathrm{I}=\frac{\Delta \mathrm{Q}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\mathrm{neAv}_{\mathrm{d}}$

\Rightarrow v_d = \frac{I}{n e A}

Since the two cylindrical rods are connected in series, the same steady current $I$ flows through both rods

I_L = I_R = I

For the left rod radius is $r_L = r \Rightarrow A_L = \pi r_L^2 = \pi r^2 =$ area of cross-section of left rod.

Electron density is $n_L = 2n$

Then drift velocity of left rod is

v_L = \frac{I}{n_L e A_L} = \frac{I}{(2n)e(\pi r^2)} = \frac{I}{2\pi n e r^2}

For the right rod radius is $r_R = 2r \Rightarrow A_R = \pi r_R^2 = \pi (2r)^2 = 4\pi r^2$ area of cross-section of left rod.

Electron density is $n_R = n$

Then drift velocity of right rod is

solution:

  • Electric Force: When an external electric field $\vec{E}$ is applied across the conductor, each electron experiences an electric force given by $\vec{F} = -e\vec{E}$ (where $-e$ is the charge of an electron).

  • Drift Velocity: The negative sign in the force equation means the force acts in the exact opposite direction of the applied electric field. Therefore, while the electrons still move randomly, they slowly drift in a direction opposite to the applied electric field.

Current in terms of $\mathrm{J}_0$ is given by $\mathrm{n}\left(\frac{\mathrm{J}_0}{6}\right)$ then value of n will be.
solution:
Let a cylindrical conductor of radius R whose axis is the line $\mathrm{r}=0$. The current density $\mathrm{J}(\mathrm{r})$ depends only on the radial distance r from the axis, $\mathrm{J}=\mathrm{J}_0\left(1-\frac{\mathrm{r}}{\mathrm{R}}\right)$.

For an infinitesimal circular ring of radius $r$ and radial thickness $dr$ centered on the cylinder's axis.

The area of this elemental ring is $dA = 2\pi r\,dr$

Since the current density $J(r)$ is perpendicular to the cross-section everywhere, the differential current $dI$ flowing through this elemental area is,

dI = J(r)dA = J_0\left(1 - \frac{r}{R}\right)(2\pi r\,dr)

The total current is the sum of all differential current $dI$ from the central axis ($r = 0$) to the outer surface ($r = R$),

I = \int\limits_{0}^{R} 2\pi J_0\left(1 - \frac{r}{R}\right) r\,dr \Rightarrow I = 2\pi J_0 \int\limits_{0}^{R} \left(r - \frac{r^2}{R}\right)dr

I = 2\pi J_0 \left[\left.\frac{r^2}{2}\right|_{0}^{R} - \frac{1}{R}\left.\frac{r^3}{3}\right|_{0}^{R}\right] = 2\pi J_0 \left[\frac{R^2}{2} - \frac{R^2}{3}\right]

I = \frac{2\pi J_0 R^2}{6} = \frac{\pi J_0 R^2}{3}

The radius of cylinder is given as $R = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}$.

I = \frac{\pi J_0 R^2}{3} = \frac{\pi J_0}{3} \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^2 = \frac{\pi J_0}{3} \times \frac{4}{\pi}

I = \frac{4J_0}{3} = \frac{nJ_0}{6} \Rightarrow n = \frac{6 \times 4}{3} = 8

Therefore, the correct answer is 8.

Find the velocity (in $\mathrm{cm} / \mathrm{s}$ ) of positive ions moving towards cathode.
solution:
Let free electrons of charge $\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{e}}=-\mathrm{e}$, number density $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{e}}$, drifting towards the anode with velocity $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{e}}$.

And singly charged positive ions of charge $\mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{i}}=+\mathrm{e}$, number density $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{i}}$, drifting towards the cathode with velocity $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{i}}$.

The current density $\vec{J}$ is the net charge flowing per unit area per unit time. $\vec{J}=\sum \mathrm{q}_{\mathrm{k}} \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{k}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}_{\mathrm{k}}$

Taking the reference direction from anode to cathode, positive ions move in the direction from anode to cathode, so their motion creates a positive current density.

\mathrm{J}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{i}} \mathrm{e} \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{i}}

Electrons move in the opposite direction (from cathode to anode). Because electrons carry negative charge (-e), their flow towards the anode corresponds to a conventional positive current flowing towards the cathode.

\mathrm{J}_{\mathrm{e}}=(-\mathrm{e}) \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{e}}\left(-\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{e}}\right)=\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{ev}_{\mathrm{e}}

The total current density directed from anode to cathode is,

J = J_e + J_i = n_e e v_e + n_i e v_i

Since the number densities are equal ($n_e = n_i = n$)

J = n e (v_e + v_i)

Number density

n = 5 \times 10^7\ \text{particles/cm}^3 = 5 \times 10^7 \times 10^6\ \text{particles/m}^3 = 5 \times 10^{13}\ \textm^{-3}

The elementary charge is $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$

And the speed of electrons $v_e = 0.4\ \text{m/s}$

The total current density is $J = 4\mu\text{A/m}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{A/m}^2$

Putting the values,

J = (5 \times 10^{13}) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}) \times (0.4 + v_i)

4 \times 10^{-6} = 8 \times 10^{-6}(0.4 + v_i)

0.4 + v_i = \left(\frac{4}{8}\right) = 0.5

v_i = 0.1\ \text{m/s} = 10\ \text{cm/s}

Therefore, the correct answer is 10.

question: Total momentum of electrons in a straight wire of length l carrying a current I is P . If mass of electron is doubled keeping its charge constant and length of the wire is also doubled keeping current constant, then new value of momentum becomes nP . So the value of n will be :
solution:
Let l be the length of the wire, A be the uniform cross-sectional area of the wire, $\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{e}}$ be the number density of conduction electrons (electrons per unit volume), e be the charge of an electron., m be the mass of an electron and $\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d}}$ be the drift velocity of the electrons.

The total volume of the wire is $\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{A} \cdot \mathrm{l}$

The total number of free conduction electrons N in the wire is $\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{e}} \cdot \mathrm{V}=\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{Al}$

Due to their drift motion, each electron carries momentum $\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{e}}=\mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{d}}$

Since the random thermal velocities average to zero vectorially, the total momentum P of all free conduction electrons in the wire is $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{e}}=\left(\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{Al}\right)\left(\mathrm{mv}_{\mathrm{d}}\right)$

P=m \cdot\left(n_e e A v_d\right) \cdot \frac{l}{e}

The electric current I passing through the conductor is $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{e}} \mathrm{eAv}_{\mathrm{d}}$

\Rightarrow \mathrm{P}=\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{e}} \cdot \mathrm{I} \cdot \mathrm{l} \Rightarrow \mathrm{P} \propto \mathrm{~m} \cdot \mathrm{l} \cdot \frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{e}}

The mass of an electron is doubled: $\mathrmm^{\prime}=2 \mathrm{~m}$

The length of the wire is doubled: $\mathrml^{\prime}=2 \mathrm{l}$

The electric current is kept constant: $\mathrmI^{\prime}=\mathrm{I}$

The charge of the electron is kept constant: $e' = e$

Let the new total momentum be $P'$,

P' = \frac{m'}{e'} \cdot I' \cdot l' = \frac{2m}{e} \cdot I \cdot (2l) = 4\left(\frac{m}{e} \cdot I \cdot l\right) = 4P

P' = nP = 4P \Rightarrow n = 4

Therefore, the value of $n$ is 4.

question: A beam of fast moving electrons having cross-sectional area $\mathrm{A}=1 \mathrm{~cm}^2$ falls normally on a flat surface. The electrons are absorbed by the surface and the average pressure exerted by the electrons on this surface is found to be $\mathrm{p}=9.1 \mathrm{~Pa}$. If the electrons are moving with a speed $\mathrm{v}=8 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$, then find the effective current (in A) through any cross-section of the electron beam. (mass of electron $=9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}$ )
solution:
Let n be the number density of electrons in the beam (electrons per unit volume).

The mass of an electron is $\mathrm{m}=9.1 \times 10^{-31} \mathrm{~kg}$

The speed of the electrons is $\mathrm{v}=8 \times 10^7 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

The cross-sectional area of the beam is $\mathrm{A}=1 \mathrm{~cm}^2=1 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~m}^2$

In a time interval $\Delta t$, the electrons that strike the flat surface are those contained within a cylindrical volume of length $\Delta x = v\Delta t$.

\Delta V = A \cdot \Delta x = A v\Delta t

The total number of electrons striking the surface in time $\Delta t$ is,

\Delta N = n \cdot \Delta V = n A v\Delta t

Each electron carries initial linear momentum $p_i = mv$

Since the electrons are completely absorbed by the flat surface, their final momentum is zero $p_f = 0$

The magnitude of change in momentum of each electron is $|\Delta p| = mv$

The total change in momentum transferred to the flat surface in time $\Delta t$ is

\Delta P_{\text{total}} = \Delta N \cdot (mv) = (nAv\Delta t)(mv) = nmAv^2\Delta t

By Newton's second law, the average force exerted on the flat surface is $F = \frac{\Delta P_{\text{total}}}{\Delta t} = nmAv^2$

The average pressure $p$ exerted on the surface is the perpendicular force per unit area

p = \frac{F}{A} = \frac{nmAv^2}{A} = nmv^2

p = nmv^2 = (nv)(mv) \Rightarrow nv = \frac{p}{mv}

The total charge transferred through any cross-section of the beam in time interval $\Delta t$ is:

\Delta q = \Delta N \cdot e = (nAv\Delta t)e

Here $e$ is the elementary charge ($e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}$).

The electric current $I$ is $I = \frac{\Delta q}{\Delta t} = neAv$

Substituting $nv = \frac{p}{mv}$ this into the expression for current $I$,

I = eA(nv) = eA\left(\frac{p}{mv}\right) = \frac{epA}{mv}

The pressure is $p = 9.1\,\text{Pa} = 9.1\,\text{N/m}^2$

Substituting the values,

\text{I}=\frac{(1.6\times 10^{-19})\times (9.1)\times (10^{-4})}{(9.1\times 10^{-31})\times (8\times 10^{7})}

\text{I}=\frac{1.6\times 10^{-19}\times 10^{-4}}{8\times 10^{7}\times 10^{-31}}

\text{I}=\frac{1.6\times 10^{-23}}{8\times 10^{-24}}=\frac{1.6}{8}\times 10^{-23-(-24)}=0.2\times 10^{1}=2\text{ A}

Therefore, the amount of current due to electron beam is 2 A.

q: Electric field, in a straight solid uniform cylindrical conductor of radius $\mathrm{R}=2 \mathrm{~cm}$ is along the axis of the cylinder and is given by $\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{Kr}$ where $\mathrm{K}=1 \times 10^8$ and r is the distance from the axis of the cylinder. If current in the cylinder is $\mathrm{I}=16 \pi$ micro ampere and the specific conductivity $\sigma=\mathrm{z} \times 10^{-8}$, find the value of z. [Read $\sigma=\mathrm{z} \times 10^{-8}$ (in S.I Units.)]
question: Electric field, in a straight solid uniform cylindrical conductor of radius $\mathrm{R}=2 \mathrm{~cm}$ is along the axis of the cylinder and is given by $\mathrm{E}=\mathrm{Kr}$ where $\mathrm{K}=1 \times 10^8$ and r is the distance from the axis of the cylinder. If current in the cylinder is $\mathrm{I}=16 \pi$ micro ampere and the specific conductivity $\sigma=\mathrm{z} \times 10^{-8}$, find the value of z. [Read $\sigma=\mathrm{z} \times 10^{-8}$ (in S.I Units.)]
solution:
For a coaxial thin cylindrical shell of radius r and radial thickness dr inside the cylindrical conductor of radius R.

The cross-sectional area of this thin annular element is $\mathrm{dA}=2 \pi \mathrm{r} \mathrm{dr}$

From the microscopic form of Ohm's law, the current density $J(r)$ at radial distance $r$ is $J(r) = \rho E(r)$, where $\rho$

is the electrical conductivity of the conductor.

Given that the electric field varies with radial distance as $E(r) = Kr$,

J(r) = \rho (Kr) = \rho K r

The elemental current $dI$ flowing through this annular strip of area $dA$ is

$\mathrm{dI}=\mathrm{J}(\mathrm{r}) \mathrm{dA}=(\sigma \mathrm{Kr})(2 \pi \mathrm{r} \mathrm{dr})=2 \pi \sigma \mathrm{Kr}^2 \mathrm{dr}$

The total current $I$, from the axis $(r = 0)$ to the outer radius $(r = R)$,

$\mathrm{I}=\int\limits_0^{\mathrm{R}} 2 \pi \sigma \mathrm{Kr}^2 \mathrm{dr}=2 \pi \sigma \mathrm{~K} \int\limits_0^{\mathrm{R}} \mathrm{r}^2 \mathrm{dr}$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\frac{2 \pi \sigma \mathrm{KR}^3}{3}$

The radius, $\mathrm{R}=2 \mathrm{~cm}=2 \times 10^{-2} \mathrm{~m}$, Constant, $\mathrm{K}=1 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}^2$, total current, $\mathrm{I}=16 \pi \mu \mathrm{~A}=16 \pi \times10^{-6} \mathrm{~A}$ and conductivity, $\sigma=\mathrm{z} \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~S} / \mathrm{m}$.

Putting the values,

$16 \pi \times 10^{-6}=\frac{2 \pi\left(\mathrm{z} \times 10^{-8}\right) \times 1 \times 10^8 \times\left(2 \times 10^{-2}\right)^3}{3}$

$16 \pi \times 10^{-6}=\frac{2 \pi\left(\mathrm{z} \times 10^{-8}\right)\left(1 \times 10^8\right)\left(8 \times 10^{-6}\right)}{3}$

8 \times 10^{-6} = \frac{z \times 8 \times 10^{-6}}{3}

1 = \frac{z}{3} \Rightarrow z = 3

Therefore, the value of $z$ is 3.
